title: Lightning Is 5x HOTTER Than the Sun's Surface ⚡
description:
You're roasting a marshmallow on something hotter than the Sun's surface: lightning! It can heat the air up to about 50,000°F (27,700°C), five times hotter than the Sun's surface (about 10,000°F, 5,500°C). A giant zap crams through a path of air about as thin as your thumb, the air cooks so fast it explodes... and that BOOM is thunder. And if it hits sand, it can melt it into glass.
Thunder or flash: which scares you more?

The science: air is a very poor conductor, so when a lightning stroke's huge current forces its way through a channel only a centimetre or two wide, the air in it is heated to around 50,000°F in a few millionths of a second (NOAA / National Weather Service). The heated air expands violently and sends out the sound wave we hear as thunder. When lightning strikes sand rich in quartz, it melts the grains along its path into hollow, branching tubes of glass called fulgurites (US National Park Service). The Sun's visible surface is about 5,500°C; its core is far hotter, so this is a surface-to-channel comparison. Stay safe: when thunder roars, go indoors.
